analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to outlaw pay-for-delay drug settlements cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2023, then sat on the Senate's calendar for 22 months without ever getting a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company is sued by a generic or biosimilar maker, the two sometimes settle by having the brand pay the generic company to stay off the market for years — a "pay-for-delay" deal. This bill would let the Federal Trade Commission treat those deals as automatically anticompetitive, with penalties up to three times the money that changed hands, and would make drug company CEOs certify to the government that they disclosed every side deal and oral promise. It never came to a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers who buy prescription drugs. Generics cost 80 to 85 percent less than brand-name drugs, so forcing cheaper versions to market sooner lowers prices for consumers, employers, and government programs like Medicare and Medicaid, which the bill's findings note pay over 40 percent of the roughly $325 billion spent yearly on retail prescription drugs. Generic and biosimilar makers also gain, because they could no longer be paid to stay out of a market and would face less risk of being bought off by a brand rival.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers who buy drugs

how_it_helps.text: Creates a presumption that a patent settlement is illegal if a brand company gives a generic or biosimilar filer anything of value and the filer agrees to delay or forgo selling its cheaper version — the FTC could bring an enforcement case on that basis alone.

Attaches real penalties: parties to a violating deal can be ordered to pay the government up to three times the value they received, and a generic violator forfeits its 180-day head start on selling the drug.

Requires the CEO or lead negotiator to certify to the FTC and Justice Department that the filed agreement is complete, including side agreements and unwritten oral promises — closing the loophole where the real deal exists only in a handshake.

The bill's own findings record why this matters to consumers: generics sell at 80 to 85 percent discounts off brand prices, yet reverse-payment settlements let brand and generic companies split monopoly profits while patients keep paying brand prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the tool of paying a generic rival to preserve their monopoly and could face civil penalties up to triple the transferred value. Generic and biosimilar companies lose the option of lucrative delay settlements and could also be penalized, though they gain in the cases where earlier entry is the point.

drawbacks.text: The bill only applies to agreements signed after it becomes law, so every existing pay-for-delay deal already on the books would be untouched.

It leaves wide carve-outs: settlements where the only payment is an earlier entry date, litigation-expense reimbursements up to $7.5 million a year, or a promise not to sue all remain legal, and companies can escape liability by showing a deal's procompetitive benefits outweigh the harm — so the hardest cases to police could still pass.

The honest objection from settlement defenders: patent suits are expensive and uncertain, and a negotiated entry date can sometimes get a generic to patients sooner than years of litigation followed by a loss in court. A presumption of illegality could push companies to litigate longer instead of settling, and could deter deals that genuinely benefit consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real and large where it applies — cheaper generics reaching the market years sooner — and the design is more careful than a flat ban, since it exempts ordinary settlements, caps reimbursable litigation costs, and lets companies prove a deal is procompetitive. The main costs fall on brand-name drug companies' monopoly profits, which is the point. The weaknesses are that it is not retroactive and that a determined company can route value through exempt channels.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list of bills, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 30, 2023 with ten other original sponsors, including three Republicans led by Senator Grassley — a rare bipartisan lineup on drug pricing.

On February 9, 2023 the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment, and on March 1, 2023 it was reported out and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders — the list of bills awaiting floor time.
The bill then sat on that calendar, as Calendar No. 20, for the rest of the 118th Congress. No floor debate, no vote, and no further action ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies are better off, because they can keep settling patent suits by paying generic makers to delay cheaper competition — a tool this bill would have taken away. Patients and taxpayers keep paying brand prices for drugs that could face generic competition sooner.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Judiciary Committee, where it was approved with a bipartisan group of co-sponsors.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original co-sponsor, giving the bill Republican cover and long-standing bipartisan credibility on pay-for-delay.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-IL), Judiciary Committee chair; original co-sponsor
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of the Judiciary Committee on March 1, 2023 and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Nine other original co-sponsors (7 Democrats, 3 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on at introduction: Blumenthal, Kelly, Van Hollen, Booker, and Ossoff (D); Cramer and Ernst (R); among the total of 10 co-sponsors.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader, controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor time for the bill, which sat on the Senate Legislative Calendar from March 2023 until the Congress ended without a vote.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry whose patent-settlement practices the bill targets
against.what_they_did: Opposed pay-for-delay legislation, arguing settlements are legitimate resolutions of patent disputes that can speed generic entry; the industry has long lobbied against such bans.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 11 original sponsors included 3 Republicans among 8 Democrats, and it cleared the Judiciary Committee with bipartisan support; the obstacle was not an adverse vote but the absence of any vote at all.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate their most reliable tool for extending a drug's monopoly past court challenges: paying the generic challenger to stay off the market, with penalties up to triple the value transferred. Their gain under the current system comes from patients and insurers paying brand prices for years longer than competition would allow.

They would lose the option of being paid to delay — settlements that can be worth more than competing — and could forfeit their 180-day exclusivity or face penalties for violating deals. But when competition resumes they are the ones selling the cheaper drug, so in the cases this bill targets their path runs alongside patients' interests.

industries.industry: Government health programs and private insurers
industries.note: The bill's findings note federal dollars cover over 40 percent of the roughly $325 billion spent on retail prescription drugs, and generics carry 80 to 85 percent discounts — so earlier generic entry directly cuts Medicare, Medicaid, employer, and household drug bills.
